fields.title: Partitioning: slicing the table into parts
fields.keyTakeaway: Partitioning speeds up queries by key and makes deleting old data cheap, but degrades queries that do not use this key.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: The orders table has grown to eight million rows, and will soon reach thirty. What changes and when should you think about it?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Working with database limits is always cheaper in advance. Partitioning a live table of thirty million rows is a nighttime maintenance window and a risk; at eight million it is a planned task. The difference in cost is determined by how early the product manager heard the signal and put the task in the plan.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: [[partitioning|Partitioning]] is slicing a single table into parts within the same database. Most often by dates: each month is a separate [[partition|partition]]. Nothing changes for the code, the table looks like a single one.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **[[partition-pruning|Partition pruning]].** A query for the last week touches one partition instead of the entire table. With thirty million rows and monthly partitions, this is the difference between scanning a million rows and thirty million.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Cheap deletion of old data.** Dropping a partition is an instantaneous operation. Deleting a million rows with a regular query takes hours of work and load. Partitioning turns [[retention|retention]] from a project into a configuration setting, and this is its main un-obvious benefit.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **Maintenance in parts.** Index rebuilding, archiving, checks run on a single partition without blocking the rest.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: What it does not give: partitioning does not increase capacity. All parts lie on the same server, and when disk or CPU runs out, it does not help.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: Signs that it is time, which the product manager also sees:
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/items/0: queries for a period have become noticeably slower than half a year ago with the same logic;
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/items/1: deletion of old data is delayed because "this takes down the database for a long time";
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/items/2: nightly maintenance no longer fits into the night window.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Orders were partitioned by months at seven million rows. The reason was not speed, but retention: legal asked to delete personal data in orders older than three years, and the estimate for a regular delete was 11 hours of continuous load.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: After partitioning, deleting a three-year-old partition took seconds. As a side effect, the partner dashboard sped up: monthly reports read a single partition.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: A product consequence learned later: queries **without a date** became slower because the database is forced to scan all partitions. Order search by phone number in support suffered. Fixed with a separate index, but the lesson remained — partitioning optimizes for one access pattern and degrades the others.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: The partitioning key is chosen once and is difficult to change. It is chosen by the most frequent access pattern, not the most convenient one for storage.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Partitioning speeds up queries by key and makes deleting old data cheap, but degrades queries that do not use this key.
